clue.text: Poet overlooking lake and way for ramblers?

indicators.note: to overlook something is to miss it out, so a letter goes unnoticed and is dropped

parts.note: Sylvia Plath, the American poet
L is the standard abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A poet strolling past a lake on a country footpath built for hikers.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the L of PLATH and PATH is left; 'and' just joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A footpath is the route walkers follow across countryside, so a path serves hikers as their route.

clue.text: One with digital expertise traps idiot at work

indicators.note: letters at work are busy being processed and rearranged into something new

parts.note: ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A computer whiz catches out a foolish colleague in the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital' suggests computers, but the digits here are toes.
explanation.definitionFit: Toes are digits, and a foot specialist is an expert in treating the feet and their toes.

clue.text: Exploit a slogan to encourage retailing?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to take unfair advantage of something
second meaning, read whimsically: a rallying cry urging shopkeepers to keep selling

explanation.surface: Using a catchy slogan to boost shop sales.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second, playful reading: the phrase as a command, like 'carry on', addressed to traders.
explanation.definitionFit: To trade on a reputation is to exploit it, and read as an exhortation it tells merchants to keep doing business.

clue.text: Stunt Grace arranged in random fashion?

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; the definition is an adverbial phrase describing the same haphazard manner

indicators.note: arranged means put into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A stunt performer called Grace whose routine has been set up haphazardly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stunt' looks like a verb or noun with meaning, but it is just six letters of fodder alongside the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A scatter-gun approach is indiscriminate and unfocused, like shot spraying widely from a shotgun barrel.

clue.text: Accepted rule covering tense Swiss region

indicators.note: something covering another goes around it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a canon is an accepted principle or rule
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A regulation about strained relations in some part of Switzerland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' reads as an adjective meaning anxious, but it is the grammar term, abbreviated T.
explanation.definitionFit: Switzerland is divided into twenty-six cantons, its federal states, each with its own government.

clue.text: Opinion given on ragged material encapsulating hard musical group

indicators.note: in a down clue, being placed on something means sitting above it, so the parts are stacked in order

parts.note: your take on something is your opinion of it

indicators.note: to encapsulate is to enclose in a capsule, so one piece is wrapped round another

parts.note: tat is shabby, worthless stuff or rags
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A critic's view of a band's tatty stage costumes.
explanation.walkthrough: Take That are a British boy band formed in Manchester in 1990. 'Hard' is the pencil grade H, and tat is British slang for cheap junk.
explanation.definitionFit: Take That is a pop band, one of the best-selling British groups, so it is literally a musical group.

clue.text: Consider clearing fine jellied food

indicators.note: clearing something away removes it, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: to feel that something is so is to consider it
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Think about whether the aspic dish is acceptable to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop F from FEEL. Jellied eels are a traditional London East End dish of chopped eel set in jelly.
explanation.definitionFit: Eels are commonly served jellied in Cockney cuisine, so a jellied food is a fair example description.

clue.text: Government managed commercial area in Spanish city

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for government
to run a business is to manage it
an ad, short for advertisement, is a commercial
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: The state ran a business district in a city in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial' looks like an adjective qualifying the area, but it is a noun meaning a television advert.
explanation.definitionFit: Granada is a city in Andalusia in southern Spain, famous for the Alhambra palace.

clue.text: Requirement none expected when being extremely selective

indicators.note: being selective about extremes means choosing only the end letters of each word

parts.note: first and last letters
first and last letters

explanation.surface: A picky person sets no requirements at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for 'selective', but it points to the extremities of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A need is something necessary, the noun sense matching a requirement exactly as a synonym.

clue.text: Get a nice pot with no end of decoration for cooking meat dish

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are mixed up into a new form
having no part of something means it is left out

parts.note: eleven letters taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: Buy a pretty plain pan to bake a meat dish in.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the N from the eleven letters, then rearrange the remaining ten. Cottage pie is a British dish of minced beef topped with mashed potato.
explanation.definitionFit: Cottage pie is minced beef under a potato crust, so it is an example of a meat dish.

clue.text: What bores might do to trap old regimental figure

indicators.note: trapping something means closing round it, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: boring people drag on, going on tediously
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Tedious people might corner some aged officer of a regiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bores' looks like the subject of the sentence, but the whole phrase 'what bores might do' is the wordplay, a two-word verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragoon was a cavalry soldier, originally mounted infantry, so the word names a member of a historic regiment.

clue.text: Line put in joke with time set back part of Ireland

indicators.note: putting something in another places it inside

parts.note: to kid someone is to joke with them
L is the abbreviation for line

indicators.note: setting something back sends it the other way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A one-liner about clocks going back somewhere in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Kildare is a county in the east of Ireland, west of Dublin. 'Joke' is the verb, as in 'you're kidding'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kildare is one of the counties of the Republic of Ireland, so it is a region or part of the country.

clue.text: Vigilant owner ultimately enters a rental property

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: entering something means going inside it

parts.note: a let is a property rented out

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so take the last letter

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: A watchful landlord finally steps into a flat they let.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside A LET. In Britain a let is a rented property.
explanation.definitionFit: Being alert means being watchful and ready, which is the same as being vigilant: a straight synonym.

clue.text: Voluntary work of a speculative kind with number leaving

parts.note: OP, short for opus, is a work

indicators.note: something leaving departs, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: notional means hypothetical or speculative
NO is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: Unpaid speculative work on which some people have dropped out.
explanation.walkthrough: Opus, abbreviated op, is the standard term for a numbered musical work.
explanation.definitionFit: Something optional is left to choice rather than compulsory, which is what voluntary means here.

clue.text: Chef got in hotel in resort

indicators.note: read as re-sort, it means being sorted again into a new order

parts.note: ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook landed a job in a hotel at a holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday destination, but split as re-sort it tells you to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Yotam Ottolenghi is an Israeli-born, London-based restaurateur and cookery writer, so he is an example of a chef.

clue.text: It could represent what one's looking for in area to shop?

parts.words: It could represent what one's looking for
parts.note: surface reading: a pronoun standing for whatever item a shopper is after
setter's reading: the two letters I and T are themselves the middle of a four-letter word for an urban settlement

explanation.surface: Whatever you want to buy, you will probably find it in town.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer works backwards: its letters would clue IT, since the core of the urban word is I-T, and the whole phrase also names a shopping district.
explanation.definitionFit: The middle of a town is its main commercial district, where most of the shops are found.

clue.text: Disown note with negative tone lacking weight

indicators.note: something lacking is without a part, so those letters go

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
NEG is the abbreviation for negative
taken as written
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: Reject a message written in a downbeat, lightweight voice.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking TON out of TONE leaves just E to finish the charade.
explanation.definitionFit: To renege is to go back on a promise or repudiate it, close to disowning an earlier commitment.

clue.text: Greek character touring a second trading area from the East for seasoned meat

indicators.note: touring means travelling round, so one piece goes around the others

parts.note: pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for second

indicators.note: in an across clue, coming from the east means reading right to left

parts.note: a mart is a market

explanation.surface: A Greek visiting a second market in the East to buy spiced meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' suggests a person, but it is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastrami is cured beef rubbed with spices and smoked, so it is a well-known seasoned meat.

clue.text: Band member starts to visit orchestral conductor with a compilation of items

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters

parts.note: first letters
taken as written
a list is a set of items written down

explanation.surface: A musician begins visiting a conductor, bringing a catalogue of pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orchestral conductor' looks like one person, but each word just lends its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A vocalist is a singer, and the singer is a member of a pop or rock group.

clue.text: One refilling a pen instinctively?

parts.note: surface reading: someone topping up a fountain pen with ink without thinking
setter's reading: an animal that by instinct herds a flock back into its enclosure

explanation.walkthrough: A pen is also a fenced enclosure for livestock; the question mark flags the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A working collie herds a flock into a fold by trained instinct, filling the enclosure with animals.

clue.text: European staff had to come out

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European
to man something is to staff it
to have a meal is to eat, so had is ate

explanation.surface: A worker on the Continent was forced to go on strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had to' reads as an obligation, but 'had' means ate and 'to' merely links.
explanation.definitionFit: To emanate is to issue or flow out from a source, as light or sound comes out of something.

clue.text: Young male left in exercise venue largely in a thrilled way

indicators.note: being in something means being held inside it
largely means for the most part, so the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: an exercise venue is a gymnasium, GYM for short
a lad is a young man
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A young man abandoned in a gym, which he is quite happy about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like abandoned, but it is just the abbreviation L.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something gladly is to do it with pleasure, close to doing it delightedly or excitedly.

clue.text: Lasting source of uplift in English novelist after bringing out one book

indicators.note: bringing something out removes it from where it was
being in something means being placed inside it

parts.note: Margaret Drabble, the English novelist

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it begins, its first letter

parts.note: first letter
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: An English author has a lasting boost from publishing a single book.
explanation.walkthrough: Take one of the two Bs out of DRABBLE, then slip U in after the D. 'Bringing out' looks like publishing, which suits a novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Something durable lasts a long time and resists wear, so lasting is a straight synonym.

clue.text: Tight-knit group not half supported by revolutionary stuff of a trite nature

indicators.note: in a down clue, being supported means sitting on top, so the parts are stacked in order
not half means only half is kept, so the rest is dropped

parts.note: a clique is a small exclusive circle
Che Guevara, the Argentine-born revolutionary

explanation.surface: A close group of activists half-heartedly backed by a radical spouting tired slogans.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of CLIQUE is CLI, placed above CHE.
explanation.definitionFit: A cliché is a hackneyed, overused phrase or idea, exactly something stale and unoriginal.

clue.text: Graduate is taken with league in Swiss city for sport

indicators.note: being in something means being placed inside it

parts.note: Basel is a city in Switzerland
a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate
L is the abbreviation for league

explanation.surface: A graduate joins a sports league in a city in Switzerland.
explanation.walkthrough: Basel, also spelt Basle, is Switzerland's third-largest city, on the Rhine.
explanation.definitionFit: Baseball is a bat-and-ball game played chiefly in America, so it is an example of a sport.

clue.text: Be in the military, switching initial directions to show bravery

indicators.note: switching one compass point for another at the start replaces the opening letter

parts.note: to serve is to be a member of the armed forces

explanation.surface: Joining the army, changing your career path, takes courage.
explanation.walkthrough: The S (south) at the front of SERVE becomes N (north).
explanation.definitionFit: Nerve means courage or daring, as in 'losing your nerve', so it is a synonym for bravery.

clue.text: Dubious expression regularly mars riffs

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so take every other letter

parts.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A sceptical remark often spoils a guitarist's licks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As if!' is said to express disbelief, hence 'dubious expression'.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation 'as if!' voices scornful disbelief, so it is a phrase expressing doubt.

clue.text: Phrase I developed for muscular pooch

indicators.note: something developed has been worked into a new form, so the letters change order

parts.note: seven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A catchphrase I coined for a beefy dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The shar-pei is a Chinese breed known for its deeply wrinkled skin and sturdy build.
explanation.definitionFit: The shar-pei is a compact, powerfully built dog breed, so a muscular pooch describes it fairly.

clue.text: Local uniform adopted by leaders of parading band

indicators.note: something adopted is taken in, so it goes inside
leaders come first, so take the opening letters

parts.note: first letters
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood outfit worn by the front rank of a marching band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' is British slang for one's nearest pub, a noun, not the adjective it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain 'the local' is the pub nearest your home, the bar where you usually drink.

clue.text: Some couples do this over start of holiday in Cuba? Not a huge amount

indicators.note: being in somewhere means being placed inside it

parts.note: C is Cuba's international vehicle registration code
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter
a bit is a small amount

explanation.surface: Couples argue over whether to holiday in Cuba, but not much.
explanation.walkthrough: O and H go inside C, then A BIT follows. In cricket an over is six balls, abbreviated O.
explanation.definitionFit: To cohabit is to live together without being married, which many unmarried couples choose to do.

clue.text: Mischievous sort rejected a flyer right away with a shabby look?

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: an elf is a mischievous sprite
taken as written

indicators.note: a thing sent away is gone, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a bittern is a wading bird
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A prankster turned down a scruffy-looking pilot straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flyer' suggests a pilot or a leaflet, but it is a bird; BITTERN without its R gives BITTEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Flea-bitten literally describes a mangy animal, and figuratively means shabby, worn and run-down in appearance.

clue.text: Former Enrolled Nurses only

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold closely, so the phrase cradles the letters within it

parts.note: spans the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A note that only ex-enrolled nurses are eligible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' looks like part of the job title, but it is a verb telling you the phrase before it holds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Mere means nothing more than, as in 'a mere child', which matches the limiting sense of only.
